Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 87, verse 1:

﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ Tasbih (glorification, i.e. declaring God free of all that is unfitting) in the linguistic sense means tanzih (declaring transcendence). The mention of "name" here admits of two interpretations. The first is that the intended meaning is the named (al-musamma) and the "name" is a supplementary element, as if superfluous, so the sense is: glorify the name of your Lord, meaning declare Him free of what does not befit Him. This may be derived according to the view of those who say that the name is the named itself. The second is that the name is intended to be mentioned explicitly. On this interpretation the meaning admits of four aspects. The first: declaring the names of God Most High free of false meanings, such as anthropomorphism (tashbih) and negation of attributes (ta'til). The second: declaring the names of God free of being applied to an idol or statue. The third: declaring the names of God free of being invoked in a state of heedlessness without humility. The fourth: that the intended meaning is the saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to God). Since tasbih by the tongue necessarily involves mentioning the name, the glorification is attributed to the name. This view is the correct one, and it is supported by what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he recited this verse he would say: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," and that when it was revealed he said: "Make it part of your prostration." This indicates that the intended meaning is glorification by the tongue together with the agreement of the heart. Since glorification by the tongue must include mention of the name of God Most High, He said: "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High," although glorification in reality belongs to God Most High and not to His name; the name was mentioned because it is the means by which glorification by the tongue is accomplished. On this reading it is consistent in meaning with His saying: ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Magnificent﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 74], because its meaning is: declare God free (of imperfection) by mentioning His name. This is supported by what is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of "sabbih" is: pray with the name of your Lord, i.e. pray and mention the name of your Lord in the prayer. As for "al-A'la" (the Most High), it may be an attribute of the Lord or of the name, and the first is more evident.

The object of "khalaqa" (created) and "sawwa" (proportioned) is omitted in ﴿ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ﴾ in order to express generality. The intended meaning is that He created everything and proportioned it, that is, perfected its creation. Refer to what we mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿Who fashioned you and proportioned you﴾ [al-Infitar: 7].

﴿وَٱلَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ﴾ "Qaddara" with the doubled letter (shaddah) may mean "to decree and ordain," or it may mean "to measure and balance things against one another." Al-Kisa'i read it without the doubling (qaddara as "qadara"), which may mean "to have power" or "to measure," and the object is omitted to express generality. If it means "to measure," the meaning is: He measured for every living creature what suits it, then guided it to it and made it aware of how to benefit from it. It has also been said: He guided humans to good and evil, and animals to pasture. These statements are examples, and the first is more general and more correct, since the guidance of humans and all other animals to their interests is a broad field full of wonders and marvels. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "He guided and misguided," and he suffices with one of them because it indicates the other. This is far-fetched.

﴿وَٱلَّذِيۤ أَخْرَجَ ٱلْمَرْعَىٰ * فَجَعَلَهُ غُثَآءً أَحْوَىٰ﴾ "Al-mar'a" is the plant that livestock graze on. "Ghuthaʾ" is dry, crumbled vegetation that has been broken up by the wind and water. "Ahwa" means black, and it is an adjective of "ghuthaʾ." The meaning is that God brought forth the pasture green, then after its greenness made it into black refuse, because when dry vegetation ages, it rots and turns black. It has also been said that "ahwa" is a circumstantial modifier (ḥāl) of "al-mar'a," meaning "the green that tends toward black," and the sense would be: He brought forth the pasture black, then made it refuse. In this view there is some strain.

﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾. This is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, in which Allah promised that He would make him recite the Qur'an so that he would not forget it. This was a miracle for him, peace be upon him, because he was unlettered (ummi), unable to write, and yet he did not forget what Jibril, peace be upon him, recited to him of the Qur'an. It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is like His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 16], and the rest of the verse. The Prophet, peace be upon him, used to move his tongue with it when Jibril recited to him, out of fear that he would forget it, so Allah guaranteed him that he would not forget it. It has also been said that "فلا تنسى" (fa-la tansa) is a prohibition against forgetting. Allah knew that avoiding forgetfulness is not within human capacity, so the intended meaning is a command to keep it under constant review so that one does not forget it. This view is weak, because of the alif that is affirmed in "تنسى" (tansa), which indicates that it is not a prohibitive form.

﴿Except what Allah wills﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first is that its meaning is: "You will not forget, except what Allah wills that you forget," like His saying: ﴿or We cause it to be forgotten﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 106]. The second is that he does not forget anything at all, but He said "except what Allah wills" to magnify Allah by attributing the matter to Him, like His saying in Al-An'am [128]: ﴿abiding therein, except as Allah wills﴾, according to some opinions. Al-Zamakhshari expressed this by saying that it is an instance of using a diminutive expression to mean negation. The first interpretation is more apparent, for forgetting is permissible for the Prophet ﷺ concerning what Allah wills to lift from the Qur'an, or concerning what Allah decrees that he should forget and then remember. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he heard the recitation of Ubad ibn Bishr, may Allah have mercy on him: "He reminded me of such-and-such a verse that I had forgotten."

﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾. This is coordinated with "سنقرئك" (sanuqri'uka, "We shall make you recite"). Its meaning is: We will grant you success in the praiseworthy matters that bring you happiness. It has also been said that its meaning is: toward the easy Shari'ah, from the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The religion of Allah is ease," that is, it is easy and has no hardship in it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 87, verses 9–13:

﴿So remind, if the reminder should benefit﴾ The purpose of this condition is to rebuke the disbelievers, for whom the reminder does not benefit, and to express the improbability of the reminder having an effect on their hearts, like your saying: "I have advised you, if you would listen." It was also said: the meaning is: "Remind, whether the reminder benefits or does not benefit." He restricted himself to one of the two divisions because the other indicates it. This (second view) is weak, and it does not have the brilliance that the first has.

﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾, i.e., he who fears God. ﴿But the most wretched will avoid it﴾, meaning the disbeliever. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Utba ibn Rabi'a, and the pronoun refers to the reminder. ﴿The greatest Fire﴾ is the Fire of Hell, and it is called "greatest" in comparison with the fire of this world. It was also said: it is called "greatest" in comparison with the other fires of Hell, since they vary, and some of them are greater than others. Both views are sound, but the first is more apparent. It is supported by the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Your fire that you kindle is one part of seventy parts of the fire of Hell."

﴿Therein he will neither die nor live﴾, i.e., he will not die so as to find rest, nor live a pleasant life. This clause is joined with "then" (thumma) because this state is more severe than the burning of the Fire, so it is as if it comes after it in severity.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 87, verse 14–15:

﴿Indeed, he has succeeded who purifies himself﴾. It may mean purification from polytheism and sins, or purification for prayer, or it may mean paying zakat. On this latter view, a group of scholars said: it refers to the day of Fitr (al-Fitr, the festival at the end of Ramadan), and the meaning is that one pays zakat al-fitr (the obligatory charity of the end of Ramadan). ﴿And mentions the name of his Lord and prays﴾, on the way to the musalla (the open prayer-ground) until the imam comes out and he prays the Eid prayer. This has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said that the intended meaning is that he paid the zakat of his wealth and prayed the five daily prayers.

Verse 18: ﴿Indeed, this﴾. The demonstrative refers either to what was mentioned of renouncing the world (tazhid fi'l-dunya) and encouraging desire for the Hereafter (targhib fi'l-akhira), or to what the surah contains, or to the Qur'an in its entirety. The meaning is that it is established in the scriptures of the earlier prophets just as it is established in this Book.
